title: Guru Nanak's gurpurab
hook: the full moon of Katak marks his birth, with lamps, kirtan and langar

segments.voice: Yesterday, nagar kirtan. Your line was the song walks outside. This week: the chaur, karah prashad, the hukamnama, the sangat, Vaisakhi, the procession. Today, a birthday the whole Sikh year looks toward. Day one hundred forty-seven.
screen: `CHAUR · PRASHAD · HUKAMNAMA · SANGAT · VAISAKHI · NAGAR KIRTAN.`

segments.voice: Late autumn. The nights are drawing in. In the days before a particular full moon, if you're up very early in a Sikh neighborhood, you might hear singing in the dark streets: small groups walking house to house at dawn, singing hymns. Then on the day itself, gurdwaras fill from morning to midnight. Lamps line the windows and rooftops. Fireworks go up. And the langar kitchens cook for anyone who comes. It's the birthday of the one who started it all: Guru Nanak.
screen: `SINGING IN THE DARK STREETS.` → `GURDWARAS FULL TILL MIDNIGHT.` → `THE BIRTHDAY OF GURU NANAK.`

segments.voice: A gurpurab is a Guru's day: purab means a festival or holy day, so it's the Guru's festival. Sikhs keep gurpurabs for the Gurus' births, their martyrdoms, and other great moments. Guru Nanak's is sometimes called Prakash Purab, the festival of the light's appearing. It falls on the full moon of Katak, a month in the Indian calendar, usually in November. The celebration builds for days. An akhand path, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, is often timed to finish on the morning of the gurpurab. In the days before, early-morning processions called prabhat pheris go through the streets singing. There's often a nagar kirtan. On the day, kirtan and talks about Guru Nanak's life run all day, lamps are lit, and langar feeds everyone. At Nankana Sahib, in Pakistan, where he was born in 1469, pilgrims gather from across the world. Here's an honest detail. The sources don't agree on the month of his birth. Some of the early janamsakhis, the life stories, place it in the spring month of Vaisakh, and some historians follow them. The Bala janamsakhi gives the full moon of Katak, and that's the date the Sikh community celebrates. Sikhs have discussed this at length, and the celebration in Katak remains. What nobody disputes is what the day is for. Bhai Gurdas, in his first Var, says that when the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world. The lamps say it without words. And Sikhs say that light didn't go out: it passed through the ten Gurus and rests now in the Granth.
screen: `GURPURAB — THE GURU'S FESTIVAL.` · `THE FULL MOON OF KATAK.` · `PRABHAT PHERIS, LAMPS, LANGAR.` · `THE SOURCES DIFFER ON THE MONTH.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT THAT CAME.`

segments.voice: Light a lamp for him. If you can safely, light a candle or a small lamp, or turn on one soft light and switch off the others. Sit and look at it. Let the flame be the only thing you watch. Think of one thing you've learned from Guru Nanak on this path: one God, honest work, sharing, the Name remembered, everyone equal at one table. If you pray, you can give thanks. If not, simply honor the light. The bell holds the time.
Gurpurab. A Guru's festival day. Guru Nanak's, on the full moon of Katak, is kept with lamps, kirtan and langar.
Your line: the light that came. Tonight, when you switch on a light, remember one person who brought light into your life, and thank them if you can. Day one hundred forty-seven.

what it means: the Guru's festival: lamps, kirtan and langar for the light Sikhs say came into the world with him.
what a scholar hears: the Puratan janamsakhi gives Vaisakh 1469; the Katak date follows the Bala tradition, and it is the one Sikhs keep.

notes: Birth month: Puratan janamsakhi and Bhai Mani Singh's tradition give Vaisakh 1469; the Bala janamsakhi gives Katak. Many historians accept Vaisakh (April 15, 1469); the community celebrates Katak Puranmashi. The Nanakshahi calendar debate is summarized as 'discussed at length'. Confirm the framing is fair.
Prakash Purab as a name for Guru Nanak's gurpurab: common usage. Confirm.
